framing_issues.text: If transparency matters most to you, Option C is the best choice.
framing_issues.issue: The page recommends an option. The nonpartisan rules allow no endorsements or ratings; the values guide may name who argues what, never which option is best. Delete the sentence.

framing_issues.text: Commissioner Bob Ellis, who sponsored Option C, proposed it
framing_issues.issue: Misattribution that reverses who stands where. Option C's sponsor is Barrett (P-032, P-024); Ellis sits on the commission, voted against approving the resolution (P-033) and for filing it (P-034). A reader using the values guide would think the commission's own member backs removing the cap.

The values guide (lines 130-133) is one-sided. It has a line only for Option C, in its sponsor's own framing ('transparency'), while documented arguments with named speakers exist on the other side: Ellis says the current process is 'more transparent and open than anything we've had in recent years' (P-073) and that the full Board decides (P-079); Resolution 26-0460 (Ellis, Abdur-Rahman) cites 'balanced representation' and 'earlier and ongoing input' (P-004). The justice officials' documented case for more money and a January vote (P-070, P-071) also has no line. This is not a case of unequal evidence; the evidence is archived.

framing_issues.text: The justice offices will get the extra money they asked for in 2027.
framing_issues.issue: States an unknown future outcome as settled, in the direction one side wants. Contradicts lines 14, 35, 140 and 241. Readers who use or work in the courts or jail would be misinformed.

framing_issues.text: Whether your property tax bill will change: it will stay the same in 2027.
framing_issues.issue: States an unknown future outcome as settled and contradicts line 15. Property owners could be misled about their 2027 bill.

framing_issues.text: the plan takes in $73,637,614 more than it expects to spend, adding to savings.
framing_issues.issue: Presents a planned deficit as a surplus. Lines 108, 139 and 239 say the 2026 plan spends more than it takes in and leaves savings about $2.8 million above the minimum reserve. The reversal changes how readers judge every option's room to spend.

framing_issues.text: District 2: Commissioner Dana Barrett, also on the Budget Commission. ... District 5: vacant on the Nov 4 agenda.
framing_issues.issue: The 'Who decides, and how to reach them' roster (lines 59-62) is wrong in two places: Barrett is listed for both District 2 and District 3, Ellis (District 2, a commission member) is missing, and the vacancy is shown as District 5, so there are two District 5 entries and no District 4. Contradicts lines 47, 64 and 85. Readers would contact the wrong commissioner and misread who sits on the commission.

framing_issues.text: must propose the budget by Nov 1.
framing_issues.issue: The 30-second version gives the wrong deadline. The status line and lines 14, 69 and 138 say Nov 15 (P-005). This is the first date most readers see.

framing_issues.text: adopted the budget on Jan 21, after the rate was set.
framing_issues.issue: Reverses the order of events. Contradicts line 15 and the bullet's own analysis tag, and suggests the tax rate is settled before the budget vote, which misleads property owners about when the rate is decided.
Internal inconsistency: line 107 gives the same figure correctly as $834,032,152, so readers see two different property-tax totals.

framing_issues.text: The proposal, due by Nov 15, wasn't public then
framing_issues.issue: Slightly stronger than the evidence: P-045 shows only that the proposal was not on the budget page. Other sections phrase this precisely ('wasn't on the county's budget page').
Implies the proposal will answer whether property tax changes. The rate is a separate, later decision (line 29, P-101), and bills also depend on property values (P-102).
